questions.question: State the genus of the plant Tabebuia avellanedae (an ironwood tree native to South America).
questions.answer: Tabebuia
steps: Scientific names are binomial: genus first, then species, written in italics with a capital letter for the genus.
Tabebuia avellanedae has two parts: Tabebuia (genus) and avellanedae (species).
The genus is therefore Tabebuia; the species epithet avellanedae is not the genus.

questions.question: Which cell structure stores starch? A amyloplast, B middle lamella, C plasmodesmata, D tonoplast.
questions.answer: A amyloplast
steps: Starch is the plant's stored carbohydrate and is made and stored inside plastids.
Amyloplasts are plastids specialised for starch storage, so A is correct.
Middle lamella is the pectin layer between cell walls, plasmodesmata are cytoplasmic channels, and the tonoplast is the vacuole membrane, so B, C and D are wrong.

questions.question: State the function of the thick slime capsule and of the pili of the plague bacterium Yersinia pestis.
questions.answer: Capsule protects the cell (e.g. from phagocytosis and drying out); pili allow the bacterium to attach to host cell surfaces.
steps: The slime capsule is a thick outer layer of polysaccharide or protein around the cell.
It protects the bacterium from phagocytosis by white blood cells and from drying out.
Pili are thin, hair-like projections from the cell surface.
Pili help the bacterium adhere to (attach to) host cells so it can colonise tissue and infect.

questions.question: Describe the methods that would be used to trial a drug made from naphthoquinones from ironwood wood to treat people infected with Y. pestis.
questions.answer: Test first in vitro on bacterial cultures and in animals, then use phased clinical trials in humans with safety, dose and efficacy checks, using placebo and double-blind controls.
steps: Pre-clinical stage: test the compound on Y. pestis cultures in vitro to find its antibacterial effect and minimum effective concentration.
Test in animal models for toxicity and effectiveness, to check it is safe before human use.
Phase I: give small doses to a few healthy volunteers to find safe dose range and side effects.
Phase II: give to a larger group of infected patients to test effectiveness and best dose, compared with a placebo or existing treatment.
Phase III: test a larger randomised group, often double-blind, against the standard treatment to confirm benefit and monitor long-term side effects.
Use a control group and the same measurements in each group so that results are valid and reliable.

questions.question: Name the type of biological molecule that starch and cellulose are. A phospholipid, B polypeptide, C polysaccharide, D triglyceride.
questions.answer: C polysaccharide
steps: Starch and cellulose are both made of many sugar (glucose) units joined together.
A polymer of many monosaccharide units is a polysaccharide.
Phospholipids and triglycerides are lipids and polypeptides are proteins, so A, B and D are wrong.

questions.question: Which structure stores starch in a plant cell? A amyloplast, B mitochondrion, C tonoplast, D vacuole.
questions.answer: A amyloplast
steps: Starch is stored in plastids called amyloplasts.
Mitochondria release energy by respiration and do not store starch.
The tonoplast is the membrane of the vacuole, and the vacuole stores sap, not starch granules.

questions.question: Compare and contrast the structure of a cellulose molecule and a starch molecule.
questions.answer: Both are polymers of glucose; starch uses alpha-glucose and has branched or coiled chains, cellulose uses beta-glucose in unbranched straight chains that hydrogen bond into microfibrils.
steps: Similarity: both are polysaccharides made of many glucose monomers joined by glycosidic bonds (1,4 bonds).
Difference: starch is made of alpha-glucose, cellulose of beta-glucose, so the orientation of each glucose unit differs.
Difference: cellulose chains are straight and unbranched, allowing hydrogen bonds between parallel chains to form strong microfibrils.
Difference: starch is coiled (amylose) or branched (amylopectin), which makes it compact for storage.

questions.question: Identify which labelled letter (W, X, Y or Z) shows a xylem vessel in a light micrograph of a stem section.
questions.answer: D: Z
steps: Xylem vessels are large, wide, empty cells with thick lignified walls, seen in cross-section as big round or oval holes.
Z points to the group of large thick-walled circular lumens in the vascular bundle, so it is a xylem vessel.
W and X point to small thin-walled cortex or epidermis cells, and Y points to small cells in the phloem and cambium region, so these are not xylem vessels.

questions.question: Identify which labelled letter (U, V, W or Z) shows a sclerenchyma fibre in the stem micrograph.
questions.answer: B: V
steps: Sclerenchyma fibres are long, narrow, dead cells with very thick lignified walls, giving small dark rounded profiles in cross-section.
V points to the dense dark cap of small, thick-walled cells next to the vascular tissue, which is the sclerenchyma fibre tissue.
U is a large thin-walled parenchyma cell, and W points to thin-walled outer cortex cells.

questions.question: Plot a calcium ion concentration of 0.45 mmol dm-3 on the given graph of inorganic ion concentrations.
questions.answer: Draw a bar for calcium ions (same width as the magnesium bar) up to 0.45 mmol dm^-3.
steps: Use the y axis scale: 0.4 and 0.5 are 5 small squares apart, so 0.45 is exactly halfway between them.
Above the Calcium ions label, draw a bar (or a clearly marked point) from the x axis up to the level 0.45 mmol dm^-3.
The bar should be taller than nitrate (about 0.01) and slightly lower than magnesium (about 0.55).

questions.question: Explain the importance to the plant of each of the three inorganic ions shown on the graph.
questions.answer: Calcium: calcium pectate in the middle lamella and cell wall strength; magnesium: needed to make chlorophyll; nitrate: source of nitrogen for amino acids, proteins and nucleotides.
steps: Calcium ions are needed to make calcium pectate, which holds cell walls together in the middle lamella; they also help the cell membrane work and act as signals.
Magnesium ions are a component of chlorophyll, so they are needed for photosynthesis (and as enzyme cofactors).
Nitrate ions supply nitrogen to make amino acids and proteins (including enzymes), nucleotides (DNA/RNA), chlorophyll and ATP.

questions.question: How many of three statements about lignin are correct? (1) lignin adds strength to cell membranes, (2) lignin gives waterproofing, (3) lignin can form spiral shapes. A none, B one, C two, D three.
questions.answer: C two (statements 2 and 3 are correct)
steps: Lignin is a polymer deposited in secondary cell walls of xylem vessels and sclerenchyma.
Statement 1 is wrong: lignin strengthens cell walls, not cell membranes.
Statement 2 is correct: lignin is hydrophobic so it makes walls waterproof.
Statement 3 is correct: lignin deposited as spirals or rings forms spiral thickening in xylem.
Two statements are correct, so the answer is C.

questions.question: Give one similarity, other than lignin, and one difference between sclerenchyma fibres and xylem vessels.
questions.answer: Similarity: both are dead at maturity with no cytoplasm and a hollow lumen; difference: xylem vessels form continuous tubes with no end walls for water transport, whereas fibres are narrow and tapered and provide support.
steps: Similarity: both have thick walls and are dead, with no cytoplasm, at functional maturity.
Difference: xylem vessels are wide, joined end to end into continuous tubes for water flow.
Difference: sclerenchyma fibres are long, narrow and tapered, giving mechanical support rather than transport.

questions.question: Explain why hemp fibres are a sustainable resource for making plant-based plastics.
questions.answer: Hemp is a renewable crop that can be regrown each year, unlike oil which is finite, and hemp plastics are biodegradable.
steps: Hemp is a plant that can be grown and harvested repeatedly, so it is renewable.
Oil is a finite fossil fuel that will run out, so oil-based plastics are not sustainable.
Plant-based plastics biodegrade, so they do not persist and pollute the environment.

questions.question: Using the table of global bioethanol production and a constant mean rate of increase, estimate global bioethanol production in 2020.
steps: Mean rate of increase = 67 600 / 11 years = 6145 (x 10^6 dm^3) per year.
2020 is 9 years after 2011, so increase = 9 x 6145 = 55 309.

questions.question: Explain the advantages and disadvantages of using these crop plants as a sustainable resource for biofuels, using the CO2 graph and the water, fertiliser and pesticide table.
questions.answer: Advantages: renewable, low CO2 per MJ (especially hemp at about 12 g/MJ), and hemp needs the least water, fertiliser and pesticide. Disadvantages: all still release CO2 (up to about 49 g/MJ for soybean) and several crops need high water, fertiliser or pesticide.
steps: Advantage: crop plants are renewable and take up CO2 in photosynthesis as they grow, so biofuels are a sustainable alternative to finite fossil fuels.
CO2 graph: hemp bioethanol releases only about 12 g per MJ, far less than sugar beet (about 40), rapeseed (about 37) and soybean (about 49), so hemp is the best choice.
Hemp also needs medium to low water and only low fertiliser and pesticide, so it has the lowest environmental cost; this reduces eutrophication and harm to wildlife.

Disadvantages: every crop still produces CO2 when burned; soybean and rapeseed need a high level of water and medium pesticide; sugar beet needs a high level of fertiliser (eutrophication) and medium pesticide.
Also, growing fuel crops can take land from food crops or natural habitat, so the biofuel is only sustainable if inputs and land use are low.

questions.question: Explain why the Venus fly trap needs compounds containing nitrogen.
questions.answer: Nitrogen compounds are needed to make amino acids (for proteins, including enzymes) and nucleotides (for DNA and RNA).
steps: Nitrogen is an element found in amino acids and nucleotides.
Amino acids are needed to make proteins, including enzymes such as those that digest insects.
Nucleotides are needed to make DNA and RNA for growth and cell division.

questions.question: Describe the role of the Golgi apparatus in forming extracellular digestive enzymes.
questions.answer: The Golgi receives proteins from rough ER, modifies and packages them into vesicles, which fuse with the cell surface membrane to release the enzymes by exocytosis.
steps: Enzymes are made by ribosomes on rough ER and transported to the Golgi in vesicles.
The Golgi modifies the protein, for example adding carbohydrate groups or folding.
The Golgi packages the enzymes into secretory vesicles.
Vesicles move to the cell surface membrane, fuse with it and release enzymes by exocytosis.

questions.question: Complete a diagram to show how a Venus fly trap extract could be tested in the initial stages of a drug trial.
questions.answer: Pre-clinical: tested on cultured cells and animals; Phase 2: tested on a small group of volunteer patients with the disease; the empty box is a review of the safety results before testing continues.
steps: Pre-clinical stage, "Tested on": cultured cells (in vitro) and live animals, to check for toxicity, safe dose and possible effect before any human is given the extract.
Phase 1 (given): healthy volunteers, to check safety and side effects.
Phase 2: tested on a small number (about 100 to 300) of volunteer patients who have the disease (HIV or cancer) to see if it works and to find the best dose.
The unlabelled box has no printed heading on the page, so I treat it as the review of Phase 1 safety data and approval to continue, before Phase 2.

questions.question: In which cells is a cell membrane present? A animal cells only, B animal and plant cells only, C plant and prokaryotic cells only, D animal, plant and prokaryotic cells.
questions.answer: D animal, plant and prokaryotic cells
steps: All cells are surrounded by a cell surface membrane, which controls what enters and leaves the cell.
Animal, plant and prokaryotic cells all have a cell membrane.
Option D lists all three cell types.

questions.question: In which cells is a cell wall present? A plant cells only, B animal and plant cells only, C plant and prokaryotic cells only, D animal, plant and prokaryotic cells.
questions.answer: C plant and prokaryotic cells only
steps: Plant cell walls are made of cellulose and prokaryotic cell walls are made of peptidoglycan.
Animal cells have no cell wall, only a cell membrane.
Option C is therefore correct.

questions.question: The diameter of the Valonia cell is given as 25 (unit garbled in text). Calculate the magnification of the diagram.
questions.answer: About x1900 (diagram diameter about 47 mm)
steps: Magnification = size of image / actual size.
On the A4 page the drawing of the cell measures about 47 mm across (about 168 px at 745 px per 210 mm); measure with a ruler to check 46 mm to 48 mm.
Actual diameter = 25 um, so magnification = 47 000 um / 25 um = 1880, about x1900.

questions.question: State the function of the chloroplasts in this single-celled organism.
questions.answer: Photosynthesis: chloroplasts absorb light energy and use it to make glucose (sugar) from carbon dioxide and water.
steps: Chloroplasts contain chlorophyll, which absorbs light energy.
The light-dependent reaction uses light to split water and make ATP and reduced NADP.
The light-independent reaction (Calvin cycle) uses these to fix carbon dioxide into glucose.

questions.question: Give one reason, other than the presence of chloroplasts, why this organism is not a prokaryotic cell.
questions.answer: It has a nucleus surrounded by a nuclear envelope (membrane-bound organelles), which prokaryotes lack.
steps: Prokaryotic cells have no nucleus; their DNA lies free in the cytoplasm as a nucleoid.
Eukaryotic cells have a nucleus with a double membrane (nuclear envelope) containing linear DNA with histones.
Eukaryotes also have other membrane-bound organelles such as mitochondria, which prokaryotes lack.

questions.question: Name the structure labelled X in the electron micrograph of two adjoining plant cells.
questions.answer: Plasmodesma (plasmodesmata)
steps: X points to a narrow channel passing through the cell wall between the two adjoining plant cells.
A channel through the wall that links the cytoplasm of neighbouring plant cells is a plasmodesma (plural plasmodesmata).

questions.question: Explain the function of the structure labelled X in the electron micrograph of adjoining plant cells.
questions.answer: It forms a cytoplasmic link between adjacent plant cells so that water, ions and small molecules can move between cells.
steps: Plasmodesmata are channels lined by the cell surface membrane that pass through the cell walls and contain strands of cytoplasm (and ER).
They allow substances such as water, mineral ions, sugars and signalling molecules to move directly from cell to cell without crossing a wall (the symplast pathway).
This lets plant cells communicate and coordinate their activities.

questions.question: A wheat grain has a mass of 48 mg. Wheat bran is 43% fibre. Calculate the mass of fibre in the bran of this grain, to two significant figures.
steps: Fibre mass = grain mass x fraction of bran that is fibre.
Fibre mass = 48 mg x 0.43 = 20.64 mg.
Round to two significant figures: 21 mg.

questions.question: Explain the advantages of cutlery and plates made from wheat bran compared with oil-based plastic.
questions.answer: Wheat bran is renewable, biodegradable and absorbs CO2 when grown, unlike oil-based plastic, which is finite and persists in the environment.
steps: Wheat is grown every year, so wheat bran is a renewable resource, whereas oil is finite.
Wheat bran is biodegradable, so it breaks down by decomposers and does not persist as pollution.
Growing wheat takes CO2 from the air by photosynthesis, so less net carbon dioxide is added to the atmosphere than from burning oil-derived plastic.

questions.question: Explain the role of the pollen tube and the pollen nuclei in forming the endosperm nucleus of a wheat grain.
questions.answer: The pollen tube carries two male nuclei to the ovule; one fuses with the egg and the other fuses with the two polar nuclei, forming a triploid endosperm nucleus.
steps: After pollination, the pollen tube grows down the style to the ovule, carrying two male nuclei.
One male nucleus fuses with the egg cell to form the diploid zygote.
The other male nucleus fuses with the two haploid polar nuclei in the embryo sac.
This fusion forms a triploid (3n) endosperm nucleus, which develops into endosperm tissue.

questions.question: Label the transverse section diagram of a stem to show the position of the xylem and the phloem.
questions.answer: Label the inner half of each vascular bundle (nearer the centre) as xylem and the outer half (nearer the edge) as phloem.
steps: The stem section shows a ring of vascular bundles, each divided into two parts by a line.
In a stem, xylem lies on the inside of each bundle (towards the centre or pith), so label the inner half of a bundle with a label line as xylem.
Phloem lies on the outside of the bundle (towards the epidermis and cortex), so label the outer half of the bundle as phloem.

questions.question: How many of four statements about xylem and phloem are correct? (1) both tissues have a transport function, (2) xylem vessels contain sieve plates, (3) phloem transports polysaccharides, (4) xylem vessels transport substances in both directions. A 1, B 2, C 3, D 4.
questions.answer: A 1 (only statement 1 is correct)
steps: Statement 1 is correct: xylem transports water and minerals, phloem transports sugars.
Statement 2 is wrong: sieve plates are found in phloem sieve tubes, not xylem.
Statement 3 is wrong: phloem transports sucrose and amino acids, not polysaccharides.
Statement 4 is wrong: xylem transport is one-way (upwards from roots to leaves).
Only one statement is correct, so the answer is A.

questions.question: Calculate the percentage decrease in mean fibre diameter from plants in row 2 compared with row 1, using the table of means.
steps: Row 1 mean diameter = 26.95 um and row 2 = 21.62 um.
Percentage decrease = 5.33 / 26.95 x 100 = 19.8%.

questions.question: Comment on the results of the water stress investigation, using the table of fibre measurements.
questions.answer: Water stress reduced the length, diameter and wall thickness of the fibres, and earlier or longer stress (row 2) had a larger effect than stress after flowering (row 3).
steps: Row 1 (watered throughout) has the longest, widest and thickest-walled fibres: 0.91 mm, 26.95 um and 3.44 um.

Row 2 (water stress from 1 month) has the smallest values: length down by about 30% (0.64 mm), diameter down about 20% (21.62 um) and wall thickness down about 17% (2.85 um); the SDs do not overlap row 1.

Row 3 (stress only after flowering) is closer to the control: length down about 11% (0.81 mm), diameter only about 2% lower (26.48 um, SDs overlap so probably no real difference) and wall thickness about 6% lower.

So water stress mainly shortens and thins the fibres, and the longer the plant is stressed the greater the effect, so fibres for paper are lower quality; the SDs are small so the results are fairly reliable, although the sample size is not given.

questions.question: Which of the given diagrams shows part of a cellulose molecule?
questions.answer: B
steps: Cellulose is a polymer of beta-glucose joined by 1,4 glycosidic bonds, with every other glucose unit inverted (rotated 180 degrees), and it is unbranched.
Diagram B shows unbranched chains with alternate glucose units inverted (CH2OH alternately above and below), so it is cellulose.
A has all glucose units the same way round (alpha-glucose chain such as amylose), C is a branched alpha-glucose structure (amylopectin or glycogen), and D has a branch, so it is not cellulose.

questions.question: Explain how xylem vessels are adapted for support and for transport.
questions.answer: Support: lignified secondary thickening stiffens the walls so the vessels resist collapse. Transport: dead, hollow lumens with no end walls form continuous tubes, and pits allow water to move sideways.
steps: Support: lignin is deposited as thickened walls (spirals, rings or pits) that strengthen the vessel.
Support: the rigid walls prevent the vessel from collapsing when water is under tension.
Transport: xylem vessels are dead, so there is no cytoplasm to slow the flow of water.
Transport: the hollow lumen and absence of end walls give a continuous column for water movement.
Transport: pits in the walls allow water and ions to move sideways between vessels.

questions.question: Which part of a plant cell stores starch? A amyloplast, B middle lamella, C plasmodesmata, D tonoplast.
questions.answer: A amyloplast
steps: Starch is stored in amyloplasts, a type of plastid.
Middle lamella, plasmodesmata and tonoplast do not store starch.
So answer A.

questions.question: How many of four statements about starch are correct? (1) compact shape, (2) contains 1,6 glycosidic bonds only, (3) polymer of alpha-glucose, (4) polypeptide. A one, B two, C three, D four.
questions.answer: B two (statements 1 and 3 are correct)
steps: Statement 1 is correct: the coiled, helical structure makes starch compact.
Statement 2 is wrong: starch contains 1,4 glycosidic bonds as well as 1,6 bonds in branch points.
Statement 3 is correct: starch is a polymer of alpha-glucose.
Statement 4 is wrong: starch is a polysaccharide, not a polypeptide.
Two correct statements gives answer B.

questions.question: How many of four structures contain cellulose? (1) phloem, (2) sclerenchyma, (3) vacuole, (4) xylem. A one, B two, C three, D four.
questions.answer: C three (phloem, sclerenchyma and xylem)
steps: Cellulose is the main component of plant cell walls.
Phloem sieve tube and companion cell walls are made of cellulose.
Sclerenchyma and xylem walls contain cellulose plus lignin.
The vacuole is a membrane-bound sap space with no cellulose wall, so it is excluded.
Three structures contain cellulose, giving answer C.

questions.question: Explain how the structure of cellulose and the arrangement of microfibrils increase the strength of a plant cell wall, using the electron micrograph.
questions.answer: Cellulose chains are long, straight and held together by many hydrogen bonds in microfibrils, and the microfibrils lie in parallel layers running in different directions, so the wall resists stretching and tearing in all directions.
steps: Cellulose is made of beta-glucose units joined by 1,4 bonds, with alternate units inverted, so the chains are long, straight and unbranched.
Many hydrogen bonds form between neighbouring cellulose chains, holding them together as strong microfibrils with high tensile strength.
In the photograph the microfibrils lie side by side in parallel bundles within each layer, and different layers run at different angles to each other (criss-cross).
This arrangement strengthens the wall against forces from many directions, so the wall can resist the pressure of the cell contents.

questions.question: Compare and contrast the structure of the student's labelled fungal cell drawing with a plant cell.
questions.answer: Both have a cell wall, nucleus, vacuole, mitochondria and 80S ribosomes; the fungal wall is made of chitin (plant: cellulose), the fungal cell has no chloroplasts, and it stores glycogen (plant: starch).
steps: Similarities: both are eukaryotic cells with a cell wall, a nucleus, a large permanent vacuole, mitochondria and 80S ribosomes.
Difference 1: the fungal cell wall is made of chitin, whereas the plant cell wall is made of cellulose.
Difference 2: the fungal cell has no chloroplasts (it cannot photosynthesise) while a plant cell usually does.
Difference 3: the fungal cell stores carbohydrate as glycogen granules, whereas a plant cell stores starch in amyloplasts.

questions.question: Explain how infection by the fungus, which reduces expression of genes for DNA synthesis and for phospholipid, starch and sucrose synthesis, affects growth of the darnel plant.
questions.answer: Less DNA synthesis means fewer cell divisions; less phospholipid means less membrane for new cells; less starch and sucrose means less energy and carbon supply for respiration and growth, so the plant grows less.
steps: Reduced expression of DNA synthesis genes means fewer nucleotides and DNA copies, so less mitosis and fewer new cells.
Reduced phospholipid synthesis means less membrane is made, so new cells cannot be formed or expanded as well.
Reduced starch and sucrose synthesis means less stored carbohydrate and transported sugar.
Less sugar means less substrate for respiration, so less energy is released for growth.
Overall, fewer and smaller cells are produced, so the plant grows more slowly.

questions.question: Discuss the advantages and disadvantages of increased tannin and flavonoid synthesis caused by the fungus for the fungus and for the infected plant, using the graph and table.
questions.answer: Advantages: tannins reduce herbivore damage and flavonoids inhibit bacteria, protecting the plant and so the fungus living in it. Disadvantages: making them uses energy and resources that would otherwise go into plant growth, and benefits are limited.
steps: Tannins: the graph shows leaf damage by herbivores falls in a straight line as tannin concentration rises, so more tannin means less of the plant is eaten.

Flavonoids: the inhibition zone for Pseudomonas aeruginosa increases from 7.0 mm at 500 ug cm^-3 to 8.0 mm at 666 and 9.0 mm at 1000, so higher flavonoid levels give more protection against this plant pathogen.

Advantage for the plant: less grazing and less bacterial disease, so it is more likely to survive and reproduce; advantage for the fungus: its host survives longer and keeps supplying it with nutrients.
Disadvantage for the plant: energy and raw materials are used for tannin and flavonoid synthesis, and the fungus absorbs nutrients and reduces starch and sucrose synthesis, so growth is reduced.

Disadvantage for the fungus: a slow-growing, weakened host gives it fewer nutrients; also the flavonoid effect is modest (a 2 mm increase in zone for doubled concentration) and may not protect against other microbes or herbivores.

questions.question: Describe how a drug containing flavonoids could be tested in a stage II drug trial for lung infection by Pseudomonas aeruginosa.
questions.answer: Give the drug to a small group of patients with the lung infection, measure its effectiveness and side effects at different doses, and compare with a placebo or standard treatment.
steps: Phase II uses a small group of patients who have the Pseudomonas lung infection.
Patients are randomly allocated to different doses of the flavonoid drug, or to a placebo or existing treatment.
Effectiveness is measured (e.g. bacterial numbers and symptoms) and side effects are monitored.
The trial is often double-blind so that results are not biased.

questions.question: Identify the molecule shown in the diagram. A alpha-glucose, B beta-glucose, C starch, D sucrose.
questions.answer: B: beta-glucose
steps: The molecule is a six-carbon ring (glucose) with a CH2OH group on carbon 5 above the ring.
On carbon 1 (right-hand carbon next to the oxygen) the OH group is above the ring and H is below.
OH above the ring on carbon 1 means beta-glucose (in alpha-glucose it is below), so B; starch and sucrose are not single monosaccharides.

questions.question: Which is a feature of cellulose molecules? A contain peptide bonds, B contain beta-glucose molecules, C form microfibrils, D are soluble.
questions.answer: B contain beta-glucose molecules
steps: Cellulose is a polymer of beta-glucose monomers joined by 1,4 glycosidic bonds.
Peptide bonds occur in proteins, not cellulose, so A is wrong.
Cellulose is insoluble in water, so D is wrong.
Microfibrils are built from many cellulose molecules together, so C describes the material rather than an individual molecule; the intended single feature is B.

questions.question: Which molecule contains magnesium ions? A calcium pectate, B chlorophyll, C DNA, D starch.
questions.answer: B chlorophyll
steps: Magnesium is the central ion of the chlorophyll porphyrin ring.
Calcium pectate contains calcium ions, not magnesium.
DNA and starch do not contain magnesium ions.

questions.question: Name one tissue that gives the plant support and is also involved in water transport.
questions.answer: Xylem
steps: Xylem vessels have thick lignified walls that give the plant support.
Xylem vessels also transport water and mineral ions up the plant.
So the tissue is xylem.

questions.question: Name one fibre that gives the plant support but is not involved in water transport.
questions.answer: Sclerenchyma fibre
steps: Sclerenchyma fibres are dead cells with thick lignified walls.
They give mechanical support to the plant.
They are not involved in transporting water, unlike xylem vessels.

questions.question: Describe the effect of length of time in storage on the germination of the stored seeds, using the graph.
questions.answer: Germination stays at its maximum for a period, then falls steeply, and finally levels off at a very low percentage; so longer storage reduces the percentage of seeds that germinate.
steps: At the start of storage the percentage of seeds that germinate stays high and constant (a plateau) for an initial time.
After this the percentage falls rapidly, so the longer the seeds are stored, the fewer germinate.
The curve then flattens at a very low percentage near zero for the longest times.

questions.question: Explain the advantages of two seed bank methods: storing seeds from many plants of the same species, and regularly germinating stored seed samples.
questions.answer: Many plants give greater genetic diversity so the species survives changes; regular germination tests viability and keeps a fresh stock of seeds.
steps: Storing seeds from many different plants keeps a wide range of alleles in the stored population.
A wide gene pool reduces inbreeding and gives the species a better chance of adapting to change.
Regularly germinating samples checks that the stored seeds are still viable.
Growing plants from the samples produces fresh seed, so the stock is renewed and the species is kept alive.

questions.question: 130 000 kg of bioplastic cutlery and straws is made per month, and 40% are straws. Calculate the mass of cutlery produced per year, to two significant figures.
questions.answer: 9.4 x 10^5 kg (940 000 kg per year)
steps: Cutlery is 100% - 40% = 60% of the products.
Cutlery per month = 130 000 kg x 0.60 = 78 000 kg.
Cutlery per year = 78 000 kg x 12 = 936 000 kg.
To two significant figures: 940 000 kg, i.e. 9.4 x 10^5 kg.

questions.question: Explain what is meant by sustainable, with reference to cutlery produced from avocado seeds.
questions.answer: Sustainable means meeting present needs without reducing the ability of future generations to meet theirs; avocado seeds are a renewable waste by-product that biodegrades.
steps: Sustainable means meeting current needs without compromising future generations.
Avocado seeds are a by-product of food production, so using them does not use up a finite resource.
The avocado plant can be grown again, so the raw material is renewable.
The bioplastic breaks down, so it does not build up as waste.

questions.question: Suggest two conditions, other than optimum temperature, that are needed for maximum growth of the photosynthetic bacterium in culture.
questions.answer: Light (suitable intensity) and a supply of carbon dioxide (plus nutrients and suitable pH).
steps: The bacterium is photosynthetic, so it needs light energy to make organic molecules.
Carbon dioxide is needed as the carbon source for the light-independent reactions.
Mineral nutrients such as nitrates and phosphates are needed to make proteins and nucleotides.
A suitable pH keeps enzymes active.

questions.question: Which scientist tested the effectiveness of digitalis soup? A Adolf Fick, B Matthew Meselson and Franklin Stahl, C Godfrey Hardy and Wilhelm Weinberg, D William Withering.
questions.answer: D William Withering
steps: William Withering studied the use of foxglove (digitalis) in treating heart conditions in the 1780s.
The others are known for diffusion, DNA replication and population genetics, respectively.
So the answer is D.

questions.question: Suggest how a suitable dose of curacin A for treating colon and kidney cancers could be determined in clinical trials.
questions.answer: Start with low doses in a small group in phase I to find the safe dose and side effects, then test a range of doses in phase II for effectiveness.
steps: Phase I trials give small doses to a small group to find the maximum safe dose.
Phase II trials give a range of doses to patients with the cancer.
The dose that is most effective with fewest side effects is chosen as the suitable dose.

questions.question: Describe how a double-blind clinical trial would be carried out with this cancer drug.
questions.answer: Randomly allocate patients to a curacin A group or a placebo (or standard treatment) group, with neither patients nor clinicians knowing who gets which, then compare outcomes.
steps: Recruit patients with the cancer and randomly allocate them to treatment or control groups.
One group receives curacin A; the control group receives a placebo or the current standard treatment.
Neither the patients nor the clinicians know which treatment each patient received (double-blind), to prevent bias.
Compare outcomes such as tumour size and side effects between groups, using the same measurements for each.

questions.question: Explain the conditions needed for the growth of bacteria, given that the stomach provides these for Helicobacter pylori.
questions.answer: Suitable temperature (around 37 C in the body), water, nutrients (e.g. carbon and nitrogen sources) and suitable pH and oxygen levels for the species.
steps: Bacteria grow best at a suitable temperature, around 37 C, because enzymes work at their optimum rate.
Water is needed for the cytoplasm and as a solvent for chemical reactions.
Nutrients such as carbon, nitrogen and minerals are needed to make proteins, nucleic acids and other molecules.
A suitable pH and oxygen level for the species keeps enzymes active and allows respiration.

questions.question: Calculate the percentage decrease in mean ulcer area in rats treated with omeprazole compared with control rats with ulcers.
steps: Control rats with ulcer have a mean ulcer area of 802.71 mm^2, and rats treated with omeprazole have 95.71 mm^2.
Percentage decrease = 707 / 802.71 x 100 = 88.1%, which is 88% to two significant figures.

questions.question: Explain the results of the investigation comparing the Cibotium barometz hair extract and omeprazole in treating ulcers in rats.
questions.answer: The ulcer area is smaller when more mucus is present; omeprazole and the Cibotium hair extract both increased mucus and cut the ulcer area, with omeprazole giving the smallest ulcers at a far lower dose.
steps: Control rats without ulcers have 2.28 g of mucus and no ulcer, but rats with ulcers have only 0.75 g of mucus and a large ulcer (802.71 mm^2): less mucus lets bacteria such as H. pylori reach and damage the stomach lining.
Omeprazole (20 mg kg^-1) raises mucus to 1.92 g (84% of normal) and cuts ulcer area by 88% to 95.71 mm^2.

The extract (antimicrobial, so it kills bacteria) reduces ulcer area by about 75% at 125 mg kg^-1 (202.80 mm^2) and 78% at 500 mg kg^-1 (172.80 mm^2), while mucus is 1.87 g and 2.17 g (95% of normal at the higher dose).
So the extract is effective but less than omeprazole in reducing ulcer area, and the 4-fold higher dose adds only a small extra benefit, although it restores more mucus.

The extract is used at a much higher dose (125 to 500 compared with 20 mg kg^-1) so omeprazole is more potent per mg; limitations: rats not humans, no repeats or SDs given, and the results are only from one study.

questions.question: How many of three statements about starch are correct? (1) contains alpha- and beta-glucose molecules, (2) contains amylose and amylopectin, (3) stored in the tonoplast. A none, B one, C two, D three.
questions.answer: B one (only statement 2 is correct)
steps: Statement 1 is wrong: starch is made only of alpha-glucose.
Statement 2 is correct: starch consists of amylose and amylopectin.
Statement 3 is wrong: starch is stored in amyloplasts, not in the tonoplast.
Only one correct statement gives answer B.

questions.question: How many of three statements about a cellulose molecule are correct? (1) contains alpha- and beta-glucose molecules, (2) contains 1,4 glycosidic bonds, (3) forms hydrogen bonds with other cellulose molecules. A none, B one, C two, D three.
questions.answer: C two (statements 2 and 3 are correct)
steps: Statement 1 is wrong: cellulose contains only beta-glucose.
Statement 2 is correct: glucose units are linked by 1,4 glycosidic bonds.
Statement 3 is correct: hydrogen bonds link neighbouring cellulose chains into microfibrils.
Two correct statements give answer C.

questions.question: Name two structures in bacterial cells involved in the synthesis of the enzymes that decompose bioplastic bags.
questions.answer: Ribosomes and DNA (the nucleoid or a plasmid).
steps: Enzymes are proteins, so they are made by ribosomes, which translate mRNA.
The genetic code for the enzyme is held in DNA, either the nucleoid or a plasmid.
Bacterial cells have no rough ER or Golgi, so ribosomes and DNA are the structures needed.

questions.question: Explain the conditions needed for increased bacterial growth, so that bioplastic bags decompose faster.
questions.answer: Suitable temperature, sufficient water, nutrients (carbon and nitrogen sources) and a suitable pH and oxygen level.
steps: A suitable temperature speeds up enzyme-controlled reactions and cell division.
Water is needed for metabolic reactions and to dissolve nutrients.
Nutrients such as carbon and nitrogen supply energy and materials for growth.
Optimum pH and oxygen levels keep enzymes active and allow respiration.

questions.question: Calculate the magnification of the Anopheles mosquito in the photograph, to one decimal place.
steps: Magnification = length of scale bar in the image / actual length it represents.
The scale bar measures about 46 mm on the printed page (about 164 px at 745 px per 210 mm); check with a ruler.
Magnification = 46 mm / 4.4 mm = 10.45, so about x10.5 to one decimal place (x10.4 or x10.5 is accepted for a ruler reading of 46 mm).

questions.question: In 2017, 219 million people had malaria and 435 000 died. Which option gives the percentage of infected people who died? A 0.02%, B 0.20%, C 99.80%, D 99.98%.
steps: Percentage = deaths / infected people x 100.
Multiply by 100 to get 0.1986%, which rounds to 0.20%, so B is correct.

questions.question: State the function of the nucleolus.
questions.answer: The nucleolus is the site of ribosomal RNA (rRNA) synthesis and the assembly of ribosome subunits.
steps: The nucleolus is a region inside the nucleus.
It contains DNA coding for ribosomal RNA, which is transcribed there.
rRNA combines with proteins imported from the cytoplasm to form ribosome subunits.

questions.question: Give three differences in ultrastructure between a fungal cell and a plant root cell.
questions.answer: Fungal cell walls contain chitin rather than cellulose; plant cells have plasmodesmata through the walls whereas fungal septa have pores only; plant cells have a large permanent central vacuole, fungi have smaller vacuoles.
steps: Fungal cell walls are made of chitin, while plant cell walls are made of cellulose.
Plant cells are connected by plasmodesmata, cytoplasmic channels through the cell wall, which fungal hyphae do not have in the same form.
Plant cells usually have a large, permanent central vacuole, whereas fungal cells have smaller vacuoles.

questions.question: Evaluate the three treatments used to kill mosquitoes in the hut investigation, using the table of adult offspring numbers and your own knowledge.
questions.answer: The GE fungus is the most effective: it cuts adult mosquitoes from 1396 (control) to 13 in the second generation; the normal fungus halves numbers; the insecticide has almost no effect.
steps: Insecticide: 919 against 921 in generation 1 (0.2% fewer) and 1353 against 1396 in generation 2 (3% fewer), so it is ineffective because Anopheles has developed resistance to it.
Normal fungus: 436 and 455, which is 53% and 67% fewer than the control, so it reduces the population and prevents it from increasing, but it does not eliminate it.

GE fungus: 399 in generation 1 (57% fewer) and only 13 in generation 2 (99% fewer than 1396), so it is by far the most effective because the spider toxin kills the infected mosquitoes before they can breed.
Limitations: only one hut (500 pairs) per treatment, only two generations, no repeats, so reliability and long-term effects are unknown.

Own knowledge: the GE fungus is a biological control with no chemical residue and resistance is less likely, but there are risks of the fungus or its toxin gene spreading to non-target insects such as bees, ecological effects, public and ethical concerns about releasing GE organisms, and mosquitoes may still evolve resistance.

questions.question: Name the organelles containing starch granules in cassava root cells shown in the electron micrograph.
questions.answer: Amyloplasts (a type of plastid).
steps: Starch granules are stored inside plastids called amyloplasts.
Amyloplasts are found in storage tissues such as the cassava root.
So the organelles are amyloplasts.

questions.question: Explain how the structure of starch relates to its function as a store of energy.
questions.answer: Starch is insoluble and compact so it does not affect water potential, it is branched so enzymes can release glucose quickly, and it is made of many glucose units that can be hydrolysed when needed.
steps: Starch is insoluble, so it does not change the water potential of the cell and cannot diffuse out.
Starch is coiled or branched, which makes it compact so a lot of energy can be stored in a small space.
Starch is made of many glucose units that can be removed by hydrolysis when the plant needs energy.
Branched amylopectin has many ends that enzymes can act on at once, so glucose is released quickly.

questions.question: Which is the percentage of the world cassava crop grown in Africa? A 33%, B 34%, C 66%, D 67%.
steps: Read the cassava bars: African production is about 160 million tonnes per year and world production is about 240 million tonnes per year.
Percentage grown in Africa = 160 / 240 x 100 = 66.7%.
This rounds to 67%, so D.

questions.question: World maize production is predicted to increase by 2.3% the following year. Calculate the predicted world maize production, to the nearest whole number, using the graph value.
questions.answer: 1074 million tonnes
steps: Read the world maize bar from the graph: about 1050 million tonnes per year.
Increase of 2.3% = 1050 x 0.023 = 24.15 million tonnes.
New production = 1050 + 24.15 = 1074.15, which is 1074 million tonnes to the nearest whole number (1050 x 1.023).

questions.question: Discuss the advantages and disadvantages of growing three crop plants (including cassava varieties) for human food, using the dry mass graph and table.
questions.answer: Cassava needs less water and fewer nutrients and gives a high-carbohydrate food, but bitter cassava is toxic and all cassava has little protein; maize has far more protein and few toxins but needs more water and nutrients and has less carbohydrate.
steps: Advantages of cassava: low to medium water need and low soil nutrient need, so it grows in poor soil and dry areas; carbohydrate is about 95 g per 100 g dry matter against 77 for maize, so it is a rich energy source.
Bitter cassava gives the greater yield (mean dry mass about 0.23 kg per plant against about 0.16 kg for sweet cassava, 44% more) and its bitter chemicals protect it from being eaten by animals.

Disadvantages of cassava: bitter chemicals (100 to 500 mg kg^-1 in bitter, 10 to 50 in sweet, only 1 to 2 in maize) release hydrogen cyanide that stops respiration, so bitter cassava must be processed before eating.
Cassava is very low in protein (about 1.8 g per 100 g against 8.75 g for maize), so a cassava-based diet could cause protein deficiency.

Maize: the best protein source and almost free of toxins, but it needs medium to high water and nutrients (irrigation and fertiliser) and has the lowest carbohydrate content; sweet cassava is safer than bitter but yields less.

questions.question: Which labelled structure (W, X, Y or Z) in the stem micrograph is sclerenchyma?
questions.answer: A: W
steps: Sclerenchyma has small, thick, lignified walls, forming a compact cap of dark-walled cells at the outer edge of the vascular bundle.
W points to this group of small thick-walled cells, so W is sclerenchyma.
X is phloem, Y is xylem (large vessels), Z is pith or parenchyma, and V is parenchyma of the cortex.

questions.question: Which labelled structure (W, X, Y or Z) in the stem micrograph transports substances both up and down the stem?
questions.answer: B: X
steps: Phloem carries sugars (assimilates) both up and down the stem, from sources to sinks.
X points to the phloem tissue between the sclerenchyma cap and the pale cambium band.
Xylem (Y) only carries water and minerals upwards.

questions.question: Which labelled structure (V, W, X or Y) in the stem micrograph transports calcium ions from the stem to the leaves?
questions.answer: D: Y
steps: Calcium ions are mineral ions carried upwards in solution in the xylem.
Y points to the large, thick-walled xylem vessels.

questions.question: Which cells may have secondary thickening in their cell walls? A phloem sieve tubes only, B phloem sieve tubes and sclerenchyma fibres, C xylem vessels only, D xylem vessels and sclerenchyma fibres.
questions.answer: D xylem vessels and sclerenchyma fibres
steps: Secondary thickening is the deposition of extra lignified layers inside the primary wall.
Xylem vessels and sclerenchyma fibres both have lignified secondary walls.
Phloem sieve tubes do not have lignified secondary thickening, so A and B are wrong.
Only xylem vessels and sclerenchyma are in option D.

questions.question: Explain the importance of magnesium ions to plants.
questions.answer: Magnesium is the central ion of chlorophyll, needed to absorb light for photosynthesis; without it leaves cannot make chlorophyll and go yellow.
steps: Magnesium ions are a component of the chlorophyll molecule.
Chlorophyll absorbs light energy needed for photosynthesis.
Without enough magnesium, less chlorophyll is made and leaves turn yellow (chlorosis).

questions.question: Comment on the results of the investigation into different magnesium ion concentrations in nutrient solutions, using the table.
questions.answer: Increasing magnesium concentration increased the dry mass of roots and shoots, with a smaller gain at the highest concentration.
steps: Total dry mass rises from 17.94 g at 0.01 mmol dm^-3 to 38.78 g at 0.10 (116% more) and 53.14 g at 0.40 (a further 37% more), so more magnesium gives more growth.
Roots (2.38 to 5.42 to 7.08 g) and shoots (15.56 to 33.36 to 46.06 g) both increase, and shoots are always about 6.5 times heavier than roots.
The gain is smaller for the final 4-fold increase (+14.4 g) than for the first 10-fold increase (+20.8 g), so the effect levels off as magnesium stops being limiting.

The standard deviations are small and the ranges do not overlap (for example 38.78 +/- 1.63 against 53.14 +/- 0.50), so the differences are probably significant; this is because magnesium is needed for chlorophyll, so photosynthesis and growth are limited at low concentration.

questions.question: How many of three statements about a pollen grain are correct? (1) contains a tube nucleus and a generative nucleus, (2) the generative nucleus divides by mitosis to form two female gametes, (3) can produce diploid gametes. A none, B one, C two, D three.
questions.answer: B one (only statement 1 is correct)
steps: Statement 1 is correct: a mature pollen grain has a tube nucleus and a generative nucleus.
Statement 2 is wrong: the generative nucleus divides to form two male gametes, not female.
Statement 3 is wrong: pollen gametes are haploid.
Only one statement is correct, giving answer B.

questions.question: Calculate the difference in surface area between round and long pollen grains, giving the answer in standard form with units.
steps: Surface area of the long pollen grain = surface area to volume ratio x volume = 0.160 x 25.8 = 4.128 um^2.
Surface area of the round grain = 5.03 um^2 (given).
Difference = 5.03 - 4.128 = 0.902 um^2, which is 9.0 x 10^-1 um^2 in standard form to two significant figures.

questions.question: Describe how a stem cell in a plant can become a sclerenchyma cell.
questions.answer: The stem cell (meristem cell) divides by mitosis, then specialises by switching on genes for lignified secondary walls and dies, leaving a thick-walled fibre.
steps: Plant stem cells in meristems divide by mitosis to produce new cells.
Some daughter cells differentiate, switching on specific genes and not others.
The differentiated cell deposits a secondary cell wall containing cellulose and lignin.
The cell then dies, leaving a hollow, thick-walled sclerenchyma fibre for support.

questions.question: Comment on the role of meiosis in the inheritance of flower colour, pollen grain length and pea pod shape, which are on the chromosomes shown in the diagram.
questions.answer: The flower colour and pollen length genes are linked on chromosome 1 and tend to be inherited together unless crossing over separates them; the pod shape gene on chromosome 4 assorts independently of them.
steps: Meiosis halves the chromosome number, so each gamete gets one chromosome of each homologous pair, with one allele of each gene.
Flower colour and pollen grain length genes are on the same chromosome (chromosome 1) and close together, so they are linked: their alleles are usually inherited together as a block.
Crossing over between non-sister chromatids in prophase I can break this linkage and give new allele combinations, but only a small number of gametes are recombinant because the genes are close.

The pod shape gene is on a different chromosome (chromosome 4), so independent assortment of the homologous pairs in metaphase I means its alleles are inherited independently of the other two genes, giving more variation in the gametes.

questions.question: A water lily leaf has diameter 305 cm. Which is its upper surface area, using pi x r squared? A 7.3 m2, B 29.22 m2, C 730.6 cm2, D 2922.5 cm2.
steps: Radius = diameter / 2 = 305 / 2 = 152.5 cm.
Convert: 73 061 cm^2 / 10 000 = 7.3 m^2, so answer A.

questions.question: How many of three statements about structure X (containing xylem and phloem) are correct? A none, B one, C two, D three.
questions.answer: B one (only statement 1 is correct)
steps: Statement 1 is correct: xylem carries dissolved ions and water, and phloem carries dissolved sugars.
Statement 2 is wrong: phloem transports solutes in both directions, not one.
Statement 3 is wrong: sclerenchyma and phloem walls also contain cellulose, so it is not only xylem.
Only one statement is correct, so the answer is B.

questions.question: Label one permanent vacuole on the electron micrograph of leaf mesophyll cells.
questions.answer: Draw a label line to one of the large clear (white) sacs in the middle of a cell, bounded by a membrane, and write "permanent vacuole".
steps: A permanent vacuole is a large, fluid-filled sac in the cell, bounded by the tonoplast, which appears as a big pale/empty area.
In the micrograph the cells contain several very large white spaces occupying most of each cell; label any one of them, with the line ending inside the white area.
Do not label the small dark oval chloroplasts around the edge of the cell or the small vesicles.

questions.question: Give two functions of a vacuole.
questions.answer: Maintains turgor pressure to support the cell and stores sugars, ions, pigments and waste in the sap.
steps: Vacuoles contain cell sap, a solution of sugars, ions and other solutes.
The vacuole maintains turgor by taking up water, pressing the cell membrane against the wall to support the plant.
The vacuole stores sugars, mineral ions, pigments and waste products.

questions.question: Draw and label a capsule and two pili on the student's diagram of a prokaryotic cell.
questions.answer: Draw a thick layer (capsule) outside and around the whole cell wall, labelled capsule, and two short thin hair-like pili projecting from the cell surface, labelled pili.
steps: Capsule: draw a second outline outside the cell wall, running all the way round the cell (a slime layer), and label it "capsule".
Pili: draw two short, thin, straight projections (much shorter than the flagellum) coming from the cell surface through the capsule, and label them "pilus" or "pili".
The drawing should have the capsule as the outermost layer, the lines should touch the structure, and the labels should have label lines.

questions.question: Comment on the results of the investigation into the effect of sodium chloride concentration on the growth rate of two bacteria, using the graph.
questions.answer: Both bacteria grow best at low sodium chloride concentration and their growth rate decreases as it rises; B. thermosphacta grows faster and tolerates much higher concentrations than L. piscium.
steps: Both species show a decrease in growth rate as sodium chloride concentration increases; the high salt lowers the water potential outside the cells so water leaves the cells by osmosis and enzymes work less well.
L. piscium has a growth rate of about 50 to 58 arbitrary units at 0 to 8 g dm^-3, then falls steeply and growth stops at about 22 g dm^-3.
B. thermosphacta has a growth rate of about 100 up to about 20 g dm^-3, then falls gradually (about 38 at 50 g dm^-3) and growth stops at about 65 to 70 g dm^-3.

So B. thermosphacta has a higher growth rate than L. piscium at every concentration (for example about 88 against about 19 at 20 g dm^-3) and tolerates about three times the salt concentration, so salt would be a less effective preservative against it.

questions.question: Give a reason why it is usual to stain specimens in microscopy.
questions.answer: Stains add contrast so that cell structures become visible and easier to see under the microscope.
steps: Many plant and animal cells are colourless and transparent.
Stains bind to particular structures and absorb light, adding colour contrast.
This makes structures such as xylem walls easier to see and identify.

questions.question: Explain how the arrangement of cellulose molecules and secondary thickening in xylem vessels contributes to the physical properties of the cell wall.
questions.answer: Cellulose molecules are hydrogen bonded into microfibrils giving high tensile strength; lignified secondary thickening adds stiffness and resistance to compression and collapse.
steps: Cellulose chains are arranged in parallel and joined by hydrogen bonds to form microfibrils.
Microfibrils have high tensile strength, so the wall resists stretching.
Secondary thickening with lignin adds rigidity, so the wall resists compression and collapse under water tension.
Lignin also makes the wall waterproof, so water stays inside the xylem lumen.

questions.question: Describe the role of the Golgi apparatus in forming the extracellular enzymes that digest the caterpillar in the pitcher plant fluid.
questions.answer: The Golgi modifies and packages enzymes made on rough ER into vesicles, which fuse with the cell surface membrane to release them by exocytosis.
steps: Enzymes are made by ribosomes on rough ER and passed to the Golgi.
The Golgi modifies and folds the enzymes.
The Golgi packages the enzymes into vesicles.
Vesicles fuse with the cell surface membrane and release the enzymes outside the cell by exocytosis.

questions.question: Give two ways in which nitrogen from digested insects is used by pitcher plants.
questions.answer: To make amino acids for proteins (including enzymes); to make nucleotides for DNA and RNA.
steps: Nitrogen is absorbed as nitrogen compounds from the digested insects.
Use 1: amino acids are made, which are joined to form proteins such as enzymes and structural proteins.
Use 2: nucleotides are made, which are needed to build DNA and RNA for growth and cell division.

questions.topic: Structures Shared by Plant and Bacteria
questions.question: Which three structures are found in both plant cells and bacterial cells? A cell membrane, cellulose cell wall and DNA; B cell membrane, DNA and pili; C cell wall, DNA and capsule; D cell wall, DNA and ribosome.
questions.answer: D cell wall, DNA and ribosome
steps: Both plant and bacterial cells have a cell wall, though made of different materials (cellulose and peptidoglycan).
Both have DNA and ribosomes for protein synthesis.
Pili and capsules are found in bacteria only, and bacterial walls are not cellulose, so A, B and C are wrong.

questions.question: Explain two other conditions, besides water and molecules from digested organisms, needed for optimum bacterial growth in the pitcher plant fluid.
questions.answer: A suitable temperature, so enzymes work at their optimum rate, and a suitable pH (or oxygen level) so enzymes stay active.
steps: Bacteria grow best at an optimum temperature because enzymes controlling metabolism work fastest there.
Temperatures too high denature enzymes, and too low slow reactions.
A suitable pH keeps the enzymes in the bacteria active, so reactions continue at a good rate.

questions.question: Describe the roles of magnesium ions and nitrates in the plants grown in nutrient solution.
questions.answer: Magnesium ions are needed to make chlorophyll for photosynthesis; nitrates supply nitrogen for amino acids, proteins and nucleotides.
steps: Magnesium is a component of chlorophyll, which absorbs light for photosynthesis.
Nitrates provide nitrogen, which is needed to make amino acids.
Amino acids are joined into proteins, and nitrogen is also needed for nucleotides.

questions.question: Suggest one advantage of the vertical growing system over the horizontal system.
questions.answer: A vertical system uses less floor area, so more plants can be grown in the same space.
steps: Vertical systems stack plants on top of each other.
This uses less horizontal floor area for the same number of plants.
More plants per unit area gives a higher yield in a smaller space.

questions.question: Which is the percentage increase in mean fruit firmness between control cherries and cherries treated three times with the higher calcium chloride concentration? A 3.72%, B 3.97%, C 6.20%, D 14.39%.
steps: Control firmness = 4.03 N cm^-2; three treatments with 3800 mg dm^-3 gave 4.61 N cm^-2.
Percentage increase = 0.58 / 4.03 x 100 = 14.39%, which is D (A, B and C are the percentages for other cells of the table).

questions.question: Give one conclusion for the investigation into calcium chloride treatment and cherry fruit firmness.
questions.answer: Calcium chloride treatment increases the firmness of cherries, and the increase is greater with the higher concentration and with more treatments.
steps: All treated fruits were firmer than the control (4.03), and firmness rose with each extra treatment.
At each number of treatments the 3800 mg dm^-3 solution gave firmer fruit than the 950 mg dm^-3 solution (e.g. 4.61 against 4.19 after three treatments).

questions.question: Explain the effect of calcium ion concentration on the firmness of cherry fruits, using the table of results.
questions.answer: Calcium ions form calcium pectate in the middle lamella, which holds cell walls together; more calcium gives more calcium pectate, so the cell walls and fruit are firmer.
steps: Calcium ions are needed to make calcium pectate, which cements neighbouring cell walls together in the middle lamella and strengthens the cell wall, so cells are held together more firmly.

The higher concentration (3800 mg dm^-3) gives a larger increase than 950 mg dm^-3 (14.4% against 4.0% after three treatments), and more treatments give more increase, so more calcium ions mean more calcium pectate and firmer fruit.
Firmer fruit resists damage and has a longer shelf life.

questions.question: Diameters: corpse lily flower 100 cm, Wolffia globosa flower 50 um. Which is the ratio of diameters? A 20:1, B 200:1, C 2000:1, D 20 000:1.
steps: Convert 100 cm to micrometres: 100 cm = 1 m = 1 000 000 um.
So the ratio is 20 000 : 1, answer D.

questions.question: State what is meant by the term tissue.
questions.answer: A group of similar cells working together to perform a specific function.
steps: Cells are the basic units of living organisms.
A tissue is a group of cells with similar structure.
The cells work together to carry out a specific function.

questions.question: Suggest how the corpse lily plant, which has no chloroplasts, obtains sucrose from the phloem of the vine plant.
questions.answer: The parasite's cells have a lower sucrose concentration than the phloem sieve tubes, so sucrose moves into them by facilitated diffusion or active co-transport through membrane proteins.
steps: Corpse lily cells have no chloroplasts, so they cannot make their own sugar and must absorb it.
Sucrose is more concentrated in the vine phloem sieve tubes than in the parasite's cells.
Sucrose moves down its concentration gradient by facilitated diffusion through carrier or channel proteins.
Co-transport with hydrogen ions (active transport) can move sucrose against a gradient when needed.
This allows the corpse lily to absorb sucrose from the vine phloem.

questions.question: Explain the purpose of the gel used in the wound healing treatments applied to the rats.
questions.answer: The gel is a carrier that holds the extract on the wound; group 1 (gel with no extract) is the control that shows any effect of the gel itself, so that differences are due to the extract.
steps: The gel acts as a vehicle for applying the extract to the wound and keeping it in contact with the skin, so the extract is applied in the same way each time.
All four groups have gel, so the gel is a controlled variable and only the extract (or current treatment) differs.
Group 1 (gel + no extract) is a control: it shows the healing time with no extract (21.67 days) so that the effect of the extract can be seen, and shows that the gel itself does not speed up healing.
The gel may also keep the wound moist and covered.

questions.question: Comment on the results of the wound healing investigation into corpse lily extract using four groups of rats.
questions.answer: The extract shortens healing time (about 27% with 5% and 32% with 10%) but it is less effective than the current wound treatment (43% shorter).
steps: Group 1 (gel only) healed in 21.67 days; the 5% extract took 15.83 days (27% less) and the 10% extract 14.67 days (32% less), so the extract speeds up healing.
The higher extract concentration healed slightly faster (about 1.2 days faster), so the effect increases with concentration but only a little.
The current treatment gave the shortest time, 12.33 days (43% less than the control) and 2.3 days faster than the 10% extract, so the extract is not better than current treatment.
The standard deviations are small (0.31 to 0.56) and the mean plus or minus SD ranges do not overlap between groups, so the differences are probably significant.
Limitations: only six rats per group and only two concentrations were tested, and rats are not humans; higher concentrations might work better.

questions.question: A spherical calabash fruit is cut in half to make two bowls, each with radius 25 cm. Calculate the volume of one bowl to the nearest whole number.
steps: Each bowl is a hemisphere, half of a sphere.
Volume of a sphere = 4/3 x pi x r^3 = 4/3 x pi x 25^3 = 65 449.8 cm^3.
Volume of one bowl = 65 449.8 / 2 = 32 724.9 cm^3.
To the nearest whole number: 32 725 cm^3.

questions.question: Explain why bowls made from calabash fruits are a sustainable resource.
questions.answer: Calabash is a plant that can be grown again each year, and the bowls are made from a natural product that biodegrades rather than from finite oil.
steps: Calabash plants are grown each year, so the fruit is a renewable resource.
Using the fruit does not use up a finite fossil fuel.
The bowls are biodegradable, so they do not persist as waste.

questions.question: How many of three statements about sclerenchyma fibres are correct? (1) provide support, (2) used to translocate organic solutes, (3) used to transport water and mineral ions. A none, B one, C two, D three.
questions.answer: B one (only statement 1 is correct)
steps: Statement 1 is correct: sclerenchyma fibres give mechanical support.
Statement 2 is wrong: translocation of organic solutes is done by phloem sieve tubes.
Statement 3 is wrong: water and mineral ions are transported by xylem vessels.
So only one statement is correct: answer B.

questions.question: Compare and contrast the structures of phloem sieve tubes and xylem vessels.
questions.answer: Both are long tubes for transport made of cells joined end to end; sieve tubes are living with sieve plates and companion cells and carry sugars both ways, xylem vessels are dead, lignified and carry water and ions one way.
steps: Similarity: both are continuous tubes made of cells joined end to end for transport.
Difference: phloem sieve tubes are living cells with sieve plates, xylem vessels are dead with no end walls.
Difference: phloem sieve tubes have companion cells; xylem vessels have no companion cells.
Difference: xylem walls are lignified, while phloem sieve tubes have only cellulose walls.
Difference: phloem transports sugars in both directions, while xylem transports water and ions upwards only.

questions.question: Explain the conditions that would result in the greatest bacterial growth on the surface of a chopping board.
questions.answer: Warm temperature near 37 C, moisture, a supply of food residues as nutrients, and a neutral pH with oxygen available.
steps: Warm temperatures close to 37 C give the fastest enzyme-controlled growth and division.
Moisture is needed because bacteria need water for metabolic reactions.
Food residues on the board supply carbon and nitrogen nutrients.
A near-neutral pH and suitable oxygen level keep enzymes working well.

questions.question: Explain why boards made from oil-based plastics are not considered sustainable.
questions.answer: Oil is a finite, non-renewable resource, and oil-based plastics do not biodegrade, so they persist as pollution.
steps: Oil-based plastics are made from crude oil, which is a finite, non-renewable fossil fuel.
Oil-based plastics are not biodegradable, so they persist in the environment for a long time.
They therefore cannot meet present needs without reducing resources or harming future generations.

questions.question: Comment on the results of the investigation into bacterial survival on pine, spruce and plastic chopping boards, using the graph.
questions.answer: Bacterial numbers fall with time on all boards, but pine has the fewest survivors at every time and plastic the most.
steps: On all three materials the number of surviving bacteria decreases between 1 h, 4 h and 24 h.
Pine: about 240 at 1 h, 57 at 4 h and only about 5 at 24 h (about 98% fewer), the lowest at every time.
Spruce: about 400, 300 and 107, a fall of about 73%; plastic: about 400 at 1 h and still about 400 at 4 h, then about 115 at 24 h, so plastic has the highest survival at 4 h and 24 h.
So pine is the best at killing bacteria and plastic the worst, with spruce between (similar to plastic at 24 h).

questions.question: Suggest one reason for the difference in bacterial survival on the pine chopping board and on the plastic chopping board.
questions.answer: Pine wood contains antimicrobial chemicals (such as resins) that kill bacteria, but plastic does not.
steps: Pine wood contains natural antibacterial substances (resin, terpenes, phenolic compounds) that kill or inhibit bacteria, whereas plastic has no such chemicals.
Alternatively, the porous wood absorbs water so the surface dries out, while the smooth, non-porous plastic stays moist and lets bacteria survive.

questions.question: Comment on the antimicrobial properties of the Heliconia extract, using the table of zone of inhibition diameters.
questions.answer: The extract has an antimicrobial effect on all three bacteria, and a higher concentration gives a bigger zone of inhibition.
steps: The control disc (0 ug cm^-3) gives no zone of inhibition (0.0 mm), so the clear zones are due to the extract and not the disc.

The extract inhibits the growth of all three types of bacteria: at 25 ug cm^-3 the zones are about 7 mm to 8 mm, and at 50 ug cm^-3 they are 12.9 mm to 14.0 mm, so doubling the concentration almost doubles the diameter of the zone.
The effect is similar on all three (bacteria A slightly the most sensitive with 14.0 mm at 50), so the extract is broad-spectrum.
This suggests the extract could be used as a source of antibiotics, but a zone of inhibition does not show whether it kills bacteria or just stops their growth.

questions.question: Evaluate the results comparing the duration of headaches in volunteers treated with new drug A and standard drug B, using the graph.
questions.answer: Drug A reduces headache duration as dose increases (6.9 to 2.9), and it is at least as effective as drug B, but the differences between A and B are not significant.
steps: Drug A: mean duration of headaches falls from about 6.9 with no drug to 5.3 at 50 mg kg^-1, 4.9 at 100, 3.7 at 200 and 2.9 at 400 mg kg^-1 (a 58% reduction), with a larger fall at low doses and a smaller fall at high doses.
Drug A at 200 mg kg^-1 (3.7) and 400 mg kg^-1 (2.9) is slightly lower than drug B (4.2 and 3.1), so drug A is a little more effective.
But the error bars of A and B overlap at both concentrations, so there is probably no significant difference between the drugs.

Limitations: drug B was tested only at two concentrations; the number of volunteers and any placebo are not stated; headache duration is in arbitrary units; side effects were not recorded. More trials are needed.

questions.question: Compare and contrast phase II and phase III of a contemporary drug trial using drug A.
questions.answer: Both test effectiveness and side effects in patients, often double-blind; phase II uses a small group and finds dose, phase III uses a much larger group across sites and compares with the standard treatment.
steps: Similarity: both are carried out on patients with the condition to test effectiveness and side effects.
Similarity: both can use placebo or comparison groups and a double-blind design.
Difference: phase II uses a small group (around a hundred) to find a suitable dose.
Difference: phase III uses a large group (hundreds to thousands) over several sites to confirm benefit and compare with the standard treatment.

questions.question: Describe how scientists could determine that the bacterium found in Greenland ice was a new type of bacterium.
questions.answer: Compare its structure, metabolism and DNA or ribosomal RNA sequence with known species, and show it is genetically distinct from all known types.
steps: Examine the cell structure using electron microscopy and compare it with known bacteria.
Compare the metabolism and growth requirements with known species.
Sequence its DNA (for example the 16S rRNA gene) and compare with databases of known sequences.
A significant difference from all known species shows it is a new type.

questions.question: Explain the changes in growth rate of bacteria B with temperature and in percentage survival of bacteria C and mutated bacteria C after desiccation, using the two graphs.
questions.answer: Growth rate of each bacterium rises to an optimum temperature and falls sharply above it; bacteria A is adapted to cold (peak about 10 degrees C) and B to heat (peak about 94 degrees C); bacteria C survives drying but the mutated bacteria C does not.
steps: Bacteria A grows from about -5 degrees C to 20 degrees C with an optimum of about 10 degrees C, while bacteria B grows from about 65 degrees C to 105 degrees C with an optimum of about 94 degrees C.

Growth rate rises with temperature as the kinetic energy of enzymes and substrates increases (more enzyme-substrate complexes), up to the optimum; above it the enzymes denature (hydrogen bonds break, active site changes) so growth falls to zero.
A has cold-adapted enzymes that work at low temperatures, and B has heat-stable enzymes with more strong bonds (e.g. disulfide bonds) that do not denature at high temperatures.
Graph 2: bacteria C keeps a high survival, falling only from 100% to about 58% over 15 days (the error bars overlap at later times), so it can tolerate desiccation.

Mutated bacteria C falls from 100% to about 25% after 1 day, 8% after 3 days and 0% from 9 days on, so the mutation changed a gene needed for desiccation tolerance (e.g. a protective protein or substance), and shows the gene is needed for survival without water.

questions.question: Give three differences between a cell wall with secondary thickening and one without, using the two diagrams.
questions.answer: With secondary thickening the wall has an extra layer, is thicker, and has a smaller lumen (cell space).
steps: Difference 1: the wall with secondary thickening has an extra (inner) layer of secondary thickening in addition to the primary wall and middle lamella (diagram 2), whereas there is none in diagram 1.
Difference 2: the wall with secondary thickening is much thicker overall than the wall without it (diagram 1 has a thin wall).
Difference 3: the cell lumen (inner space) is smaller or narrower in the cell with secondary thickening because the new layer is added on the inside of the primary wall.
Own knowledge: the secondary layer is made of cellulose with lignin, so it is stronger and waterproof.

questions.question: How many of three statements about cellulose molecules are correct? (1) contain beta-glucose molecules, (2) contain 1,4 and 1,6 glycosidic bonds, (3) form microfibrils. A none, B one, C two, D three.
questions.answer: C two (statements 1 and 3 are correct)
steps: Statement 1 is correct: cellulose is made of beta-glucose.
Statement 2 is wrong: cellulose has only 1,4 glycosidic bonds; 1,6 bonds occur in branched starch.
Statement 3 is correct: cellulose molecules form microfibrils.
Two correct statements give answer C.

questions.question: Explain how secondary thickening contributes to the physical properties of sclerenchyma fibres.
questions.answer: Secondary thickening with lignin makes the wall thick, rigid and strong, so the fibres resist bending and compression and support the plant.
steps: Secondary thickening adds extra layers of cellulose and lignin inside the primary wall.
Lignin is rigid and strong, so the wall becomes stiff.
The thick walls give the fibre high strength and resistance to bending and compression.

questions.question: Describe the function of the pits in the wall of a xylem vessel, shown in the electron micrograph.
questions.answer: Pits are gaps in the lignified wall that allow water and mineral ions to move sideways between neighbouring xylem vessels.
steps: Pits are areas where secondary thickening is absent, so the wall is thin there.
Water and ions can pass through these thin areas from one vessel to the next.
This allows water to move sideways to avoid blockages and reach other parts of the plant.

questions.question: Which labelled structure (W, X, Y or Z) in the cross-section would be stained a different colour after one hour?
questions.answer: D: Z
steps: The stain is carried up the stem in the xylem, so the part that changes colour is the xylem.
In each vascular bundle the xylem lies on the inner side (towards the centre of the stem) and the phloem on the outer side; Z points to the inner part of the bundle, which is the xylem.
W and X point to structures at the edge (such as the epidermis or collenchyma ribs) and Y points to the outer part of the bundle (phloem).

questions.question: Explain why, after one hour, the half-way cross-section of the celery stem would be a different colour.
questions.answer: The stain is carried up the xylem vessels by the transpiration stream, so the xylem at this height takes up stain.
steps: Xylem vessels carry water and dissolved substances from the roots up the stem.
Water evaporates from the leaves (transpiration), pulling water up the xylem.
The stain dissolved in the water is carried up the dead, hollow xylem vessels.
So the xylem at the half-way point becomes coloured.

questions.question: Name one organelle in a leaf cell that stores starch.
questions.answer: Chloroplast
steps: Chloroplasts are plastids in leaf mesophyll cells.
During photosynthesis they make starch, which is stored in them as grains.
So a chloroplast is an organelle that stores starch in a leaf cell.

questions.question: How many of the given diagrams show the structure of part of a starch molecule? A none, B one, C two, D three.
questions.answer: C: two
steps: Starch is a polymer of alpha-glucose, made of unbranched amylose (alpha-1,4 bonds) and branched amylopectin (alpha-1,4 with alpha-1,6 branches).
The first diagram (all glucose units the same way round) is amylose and the third diagram (a branched chain) is amylopectin, so both are starch.
The second diagram has alternate glucose units inverted (beta-glucose), which is cellulose and not starch, so two diagrams show starch.

questions.question: Give one role of starch molecules in a leaf cell.
questions.answer: Starch is a store of glucose that can be hydrolysed to release energy for respiration when needed.
steps: Plants make glucose by photosynthesis, more than they need immediately.
The excess is joined into starch, an insoluble store.
When needed, starch is hydrolysed back to glucose for respiration.

questions.question: Give one reason why starch-based transparent bioplastic film is more sustainable than oil-based plastics.
questions.answer: Starch comes from plants, which are renewable, unlike oil-based plastics, which come from a finite resource.
steps: Starch is made by plants that can be grown each year, so it is renewable.
Oil-based plastics come from finite fossil fuels.
Starch film is also biodegradable, so it breaks down rather than persisting.

questions.question: Label the photograph of a transverse section of a stem to show the phloem, sclerenchyma fibres and xylem vessels.
questions.answer: Sclerenchyma fibres: the dark cap of small thick-walled cells at the top of the vascular bundle; phloem: the region of small thin-walled cells just below it; xylem vessels: the group of large thick-walled cells at the lower right.
steps: Label the dense, dark ring or cap of small cells with very thick walls at the outer (upper) edge of the bundle as sclerenchyma fibres.
Label the area of small, thinner-walled cells (with sieve tubes and companion cells) between the sclerenchyma and the large vessels as phloem.
